Chapter 7: Encounters with the Outside World—Translators, Writers, and the Struggle for Understanding.
As the years roll by, the world seems to shrink. Outsiders come more often now—missionaries, government folks, anthropologists, writers—all bringing their own questions, their own ideas about what it means to be Lakota. Some are honestly curious, while others arrive hoping to change, or even “improve,” the people they meet.
For the old man, these encounters feel like a mixed blessing. They’re opportunities, sure, but they’re also challenges.
He still remembers the first time he sat across from a white man holding a notebook. There was an awkwardness in the air—like both of them were trying to find common ground, but the ground kept shifting. Words didn’t always translate well. There were ideas—about spirit, land, community—that simply didn’t fit neatly into someone else’s language.
Sometimes, the old man felt like he was shouting across a vast canyon, his meaning just drifting away in the space between two worlds.
But he never gives up. He wants people to know the truth of his people’s experience—not as something strange or exotic, but as something real and alive. He works with translators, with writers who promise to honor his words. There are moments when he gets frustrated, when it feels like his story is being twisted to fit someone else’s expectations.
Still, there are moments of hope—moments when he sees real understanding spark in someone’s eyes.
Then one day, a writer shows up who listens differently. This one doesn’t rush, doesn’t interrupt—he just lets the old man speak in his own way, at his own pace. Their conversations stretch on for days, sometimes outside under the sky, sometimes sitting by a fire.
The old man shares stories of his vision, of the Ghost Dance, of the pain and hope that have shaped his life. The writer listens, asks questions, and tries his best to capture the real spirit of what’s being shared.
When the story is finally written down, the old man reads it with mixed emotions. Some things are missing. Some things have changed. But the heart of the story is still there. He understands that no translation can ever be perfect—some things you just have to live to truly understand.
Still, he’s grateful. Grateful that the story will be shared, that the truth of his people’s experience won’t be lost.
Through all these encounters, the old man learns something important—real understanding goes both ways. It takes patience. It takes humility. And it takes a willingness to really listen.
He realizes the world is full of people searching—for meaning, for connection, for a place to belong. By sharing his story, he’s offering a glimpse into another way of seeing things, another way of being in the world.
